# Discovering Catalina Island's Two Harbors

Kim Francis is captivated by Catalina Island's Two Harbors, marveling that such a scenic escape lies just 22 miles from Los Angeles. The proximity of this idyllic retreat to one of America's largest metropolitan areas makes it all the more remarkable—a world away from the bustle of city life, yet only a short journey from its shores.

Visitors flock to Catalina's west end, drawn away from the larger settlement of Avalon in search of a more tranquil and adventurous experience. Here, they come to hike scenic trails, watch wildlife in its natural habitat, and try their hand at snorkeling and paddling, often for the very first time. The area's unspoiled beauty and slower pace offer a refreshing alternative to the island's more developed destinations.

Among the most popular activities are guided kayak tours, which allow paddlers to explore secluded coves, mysterious caves, and Catalina's distinctive kelp forests. As they glide through the clear waters, adventurers frequently encounter an abundance of marine life, including pelicans, sea lions, and playful dolphins—unforgettable encounters that bring the island's rich ecosystem to life.

The island's wildlife extends beyond its waters as well. Nearly 250 bison now roam Catalina's rugged interior, descendants of animals originally brought to the island as film extras in the 1920s. Today, these majestic creatures are protected by the Catalina Island Conservancy, which works to preserve both the bison and the island's fragile natural environment.

For those eager to explore on foot, free hiking permits grant visitors access to a network of scenic trails. Among these is the challenging Boushay Trail, which climbs an impressive 1,800 feet to Silver Peak. The demanding ascent rewards hikers with sweeping views of the Pacific Ocean, making the effort well worth it for those seeking both adventure and breathtaking scenery.

# Escape to Catalina Island's Wild West End

Just twenty-two miles off the coast of Los Angeles, yet a world away from the sprawling metropolis, lies Two Harbors—a serene gateway to Catalina Island's rugged west end. For travelers seeking respite from the bustle of mainland life, this destination offers an authentic nature-focused escape where the pace slows and the natural world takes center stage.

## Adventures Beneath and Above the Waves

The waters surrounding Two Harbors teem with life, inviting visitors to explore their hidden treasures. Snorkelers can drift through swaying kelp forests, coming face-to-face with the vibrant marine ecosystem that thrives in these protected waters. For those who prefer to stay on the surface, kayaking provides an intimate way to discover the coastline's secrets—paddling into secluded coves and mysterious sea caves that remain inaccessible by any other means.

On land, adventure takes a different but equally thrilling form. Guided Hummer tours carry visitors across the island's backcountry, where the terrain opens up to reveal one of Catalina's most remarkable attractions: its resident bison herd.

## The Island's Iconic Bison

Numbering nearly 250 strong, these majestic animals have become an enduring symbol of the island. Their story is as unusual as their presence is unexpected. The herd traces its origins to the 1920s, when a small group of bison was transported to Catalina to serve as extras in a Hollywood film. When production wrapped, the animals remained behind, gradually establishing themselves as permanent residents.

Today, the Catalina Island Conservancy carefully safeguards this beloved herd, ensuring the animals thrive while maintaining the delicate balance of the island's ecosystem. Witnessing these powerful creatures roam freely against the backdrop of the Pacific is an experience that stays with visitors long after they leave.

## Trails and Panoramic Vistas

For hikers and outdoor enthusiasts, Two Harbors serves as a launching point for exploration. A network of trails winds through the unspoiled landscape, ranging from gentle coastal walks to more demanding treks. Among the most rewarding is the ascent to Silver Peak, where hikers are rewarded with sweeping panoramic views of the Pacific Ocean stretching endlessly toward the horizon.

## A Reluctant Farewell

It is little wonder that so many visitors find themselves reluctant to board the ferry home. With its combination of underwater wonders, wildlife encounters, and breathtaking scenery, Catalina Island's west end delivers the kind of unspoiled beauty and adventure that has become increasingly rare. For those willing to make the short journey across the channel, Two Harbors offers not just a getaway, but a genuine reconnection with the natural world.

# Coastal Living: Life With Bare Feet in the Sand

There's something profoundly freeing about coastal living—a lifestyle that invites you to slow down, breathe deeply, and reconnect with the simple pleasures of life. At the heart of this experience lies one small but meaningful ritual: kicking off your shoes and going barefoot.

## The Barefoot Philosophy

Living by the coast changes your relationship with your surroundings. Shoes become optional, almost unnecessary. Each morning begins with the cool touch of sand beneath your feet, and evenings end with salty air drifting through open windows. Going barefoot isn't just about comfort—it's a symbol of shedding the pressures and formalities of everyday life. When your feet touch the earth directly, you feel grounded, present, and wonderfully alive.

## The Rhythm of the Sea

Coastal living moves to the gentle rhythm of the tides. There's no rushing here. The ocean teaches patience as waves roll in and out, reminding us that everything happens in its own time. Days are measured not by clocks but by sunrises over the water, afternoon swims, and golden sunsets that paint the sky in brilliant hues.

## A Healthier Way of Life

The benefits of living near the coast extend far beyond aesthetics. The fresh sea breeze, the calming sound of waves, and the abundance of natural light all contribute to improved mental and physical wellbeing. Walking barefoot along the shore provides natural reflexology, stimulating the senses and encouraging mindfulness. Studies suggest that time spent by the ocean can reduce stress, lower blood pressure, and boost overall happiness.

## Embracing Simplicity

Perhaps the greatest gift of coastal living is its invitation to embrace simplicity. Life becomes less about accumulating possessions and more about savoring experiences—collecting seashells, watching the horizon, and feeling the warm sand between your toes. It's a gentle reminder that the best things in life are often the simplest.

## Conclusion

Coastal living, with its barefoot ease and natural beauty, offers more than just a place to reside—it offers a way of being. It's an invitation to live authentically, to slow down, and to find joy in the everyday moments that connect us to the natural world. So take off your shoes, feel the sand, and let the sea guide you toward a simpler, more fulfilling life.

# Escape to Two Harbors: Catalina's Wild and Wonderful West End

*Where a narrow isthmus, crystalline coves, and roaming bison offer a rugged alternative to the island's bustling east*

---

There's a moment, as the ferry rounds the rocky point and Two Harbors slides into view, when time seems to loosen its grip. Gone are the crowds and the cruise-ship clamor of Avalon. In their place: a single palm-lined shore, a scattering of white buildings, and two glittering bays pinched together by a slender ribbon of land barely half a mile wide.

This is Catalina Island's west end, and Two Harbors is its beating heart—a place where the wild still whispers.

## A Village Between Two Bays

Named for its unique geography, Two Harbors sits on the isthmus where Isthmus Cove and Catalina Harbor nearly meet. Fewer than 300 people call it home year-round, and the entire "downtown" can be crossed on foot in under ten minutes. What it lacks in size, it more than makes up for in soul.

"People come here to unplug," says Marla Reyes, a longtime dive guide who's worked the west end waters for over a decade. "There's one restaurant, one general store, and about a thousand ways to fall in love with the ocean. That's the magic."

## Paddling the Quiet Coves

Mornings at Two Harbors begin with glassy water and pelicans gliding low over Isthmus Cove. It's the perfect invitation to grab a kayak.

Launching from the sandy beach, paddlers can trace the coastline toward secluded coves like Cherry Cove and Fourth of July Cove, where kelp forests sway just beneath the surface and the only sounds are the dip of a paddle and the occasional bark of a sea lion.

"I've kayaked all over California, and there's nothing like slipping into these coves at sunrise," says Denver visitor Tom Halloway, drying off after a morning on the water. "A sea lion followed my kayak for a quarter mile. My kids still won't stop talking about it."

Guided tours are available for beginners, while experienced paddlers can rent by the hour and chart their own course.

## Beneath the Surface

Two Harbors is a snorkeler's dream, thanks to the protected waters of Catalina's leeward side. Just offshore, the state's iconic garibaldi—flashes of brilliant orange—dart through emerald kelp, while calico bass and bat rays cruise the sandy bottoms.

Lover's Cove and the waters around the isthmus offer easy entry points, but many visitors book a boat to reach pristine snorkeling grounds farther afield.

"The visibility out here can hit 60 feet on a good day," says Reyes. "You drop into the kelp forest and it's like swimming through a cathedral. First-timers always come up grinning."

For those who prefer to stay dry, the same waters make for extraordinary scuba diving, with several nearby sites suitable for all certification levels.

## Where the Buffalo Roam

Perhaps the west end's most surprising residents arrived by accident. In 1924, a film crew brought fourteen bison to the island for a Western; when production wrapped, the animals stayed. Today, roughly 150 descendants roam Catalina's rugged interior.

An open-air Hummer tour into the backcountry offers the best chance to see them, bumping along dusty ridgelines with panoramic views of both the Pacific and the mainland beyond.

"You round a bend and suddenly there's this massive, ancient-looking creature just standing in the chaparral," says guide Danny Ochoa, who's led interior tours for six years. "Guests gasp every single time. These bison have adapted to island life in ways scientists are still studying. They're a living piece of Hollywood history."

Beyond bison, the tours reveal the island's wilder side—soaring bald eagles, endemic island foxes no bigger than a house cat, and sweeping vistas you simply can't reach on foot.

## Sunsets and Simple Pleasures

As evening falls, life in Two Harbors gathers at the water's edge. Boaters row ashore from moored sailboats, hikers return dusty and content from the Trans-Catalina Trail, and everyone seems to migrate toward the same weathered patio to watch the sun sink into the sea.

"There's no rush here," says Ochoa. "You watch the light change, you have a good meal, you talk to strangers who become friends. That's the whole itinerary. And honestly? It's enough."

---

## Where to Stay, Play & Dine

### STAY

**Banning House Lodge**
A historic 1910 craftsman-style inn perched on the isthmus with sweeping views of both harbors. Twelve individually decorated rooms offer a cozy, romantic retreat.
*Reservations: (310) 510-4228 | visitcatalinaisland.com*

**Two Harbors Campground**
For the full outdoor experience, beachfront tent sites and rustic cabins sit steps from the water. Popular with hikers on the Trans-Catalina Trail.
*Reservations: (310) 510-4205*

### PLAY

**Two Harbors Dive & Recreation Center**
Your one-stop shop for kayak rentals, snorkel gear, guided paddling tours, and scuba excursions. Book ahead in summer.
*(310) 510-4272*

**Catalina Island Conservancy – Bison & Interior Tours**
Open-air Hummer tours into the protected backcountry to spot bison, foxes, and eagles. Reserve in advance.
*(310) 510-4205 | catalinaconservancy.org*

**Trans-Catalina Trail**
A 38.5-mile trail crossing the island's spine. Day hikers can tackle scenic sections directly from Two Harbors.

### DINE

**Harbor Reef Restaurant**
The isthmus's beloved (and only) full-service restaurant, serving fresh seafood, hearty island fare, and the legendary "Buffalo Milk" cocktail. Don't miss the sunset from the patio.
*(310) 510-4215*

**Two Harbors General Store**
Stock up on picnic supplies, snacks, and provisions for your day on the water.
*(310) 510-4245*

### GETTING THERE

**Catalina Express** offers ferry service to Two Harbors from San Pedro and Long Beach. The scenic crossing takes about 90 minutes.
*(800) 613-1212 | catalinaexpress.com*

---

*Whether you come to paddle the coves, dive the kelp forests, or simply watch bison graze against a Pacific backdrop, Two Harbors rewards those willing to venture west. Just don't expect to want to leave.*

# Two Harbors: Catalina's Wild Heart

*Where the bison roam and adventure never sleeps*

---

While most visitors to Catalina Island crowd the bustling streets of Avalon, those in the know point their compasses toward the island's rugged, windswept northern reaches. Here, at the narrow isthmus where the Pacific squeezes the land to barely half a mile wide, sits Two Harbors—a place that feels less like a resort town and more like a well-kept secret whispered between kindred spirits who prefer their getaways with a healthy dose of wilderness.

## A Different Kind of Island Escape

The moment your ferry rounds the point and Two Harbors comes into view, you understand the appeal. With a year-round population hovering around 200 souls, this tiny village offers something increasingly rare: genuine tranquility. The single-street settlement, framed by twin harbors that give the place its name, serves as the gateway to some of Southern California's most spectacular—and least trafficked—outdoor terrain.

The air smells of salt and sage. Sailboats bob in the protected coves. And beyond the shoreline, the interior beckons with rolling golden hills that seem to belong to another century entirely.

## Adventure in Every Direction

**On the Water**

The twin harbors aren't just scenic—they're playgrounds. Kayakers glide through crystalline waters teeming with the vibrant orange garibaldi, California's state marine fish. Snorkelers and divers descend into kelp forests that sway like underwater cathedrals, home to sea lions, bat rays, and the occasional curious harbor seal. The waters here are part of a protected marine environment, meaning the sea life is abundant and remarkably unbothered by human company.

For those seeking a thrill, stand-up paddleboarding along the coastline offers a serene morning workout, while boat charters can whisk you to hidden coves accessible only by sea.

**On the Trails**

Two Harbors is the beating heart of the Trans-Catalina Trail, a 38.5-mile backpacking route that traces the island's dramatic spine. Even day hikers can sample its glory, ascending ridgelines that reward the effort with sweeping panoramas of the mainland shimmering across the channel. The trails wind through terrain that feels almost prehistoric—canyons carved by ancient waters, hillsides dotted with prickly pear cactus, and ridgetops where you can watch the fog roll in like a living thing.

Mountain bikers, too, find their bliss here, though a freewheeling permit is required to explore the island's interior roads and trails.

## The Legend of the Bison

No story about Catalina's wild interior is complete without its most iconic residents: the American bison.

The tale of how these massive beasts came to roam a California island is pure Hollywood—literally. In 1924, a film production brought a small herd of bison to Catalina for a Western movie. When filming wrapped, the animals were left behind, and against all odds, they thrived. What began as roughly a dozen animals grew into a herd that has become inseparable from the island's identity.

Today, around 100 to 150 bison wander the island's interior, managed carefully by the Catalina Island Conservancy to maintain a healthy, sustainable population. Encountering one of these shaggy giants on a backcountry hike or during a guided excursion is a genuinely awe-inspiring experience. Standing up to six feet tall at the shoulder and weighing as much as 2,000 pounds, they are magnificent, unhurried, and utterly unexpected against the backdrop of the sparkling Pacific.

A word to the wise: while the bison may appear docile as they graze, they are wild animals. Rangers recommend keeping a respectful distance of at least 150 feet. Admire them, photograph them, but never approach. The best sightings often come along the interior roads between Avalon and Two Harbors, making the overland journey an adventure in itself.

## The Rhythm of Island Life

Part of Two Harbors' charm is its unhurried pace. Days here are measured not by schedules but by tides and sunsets. You might spend a morning diving, an afternoon hiking to a hilltop, and an evening watching the sky ignite in shades of coral and gold while dolphins carve through the water offshore. As night falls, the absence of light pollution reveals a canopy of stars that city dwellers rarely witness.

---

## Plan Your Escape

**Where to Stay**

- **Banning House Lodge** — This historic 1910 craftsman-style inn perched above the isthmus is the crown jewel of Two Harbors lodging. With cozy rooms, stunning harbor views, and a warm, old-world atmosphere, it's the perfect basecamp for adventure.
- **Two Harbors Campground** — For those who want to sleep closer to nature, this beachside campground offers tent sites just steps from the water. Rent equipment on-site if you're traveling light.
- **Boat Moorings** — Sailing enthusiasts can moor in the harbor and make the village their home port for the duration of their stay.

**Where to Eat**

- **Harbor Reef Restaurant** — The village's dining anchor serves fresh seafood, hearty steaks, and Catalina classics in a laid-back setting. Don't leave without trying a signature **Buffalo Milk**—a creamy, indulgent cocktail that's become the island's unofficial drink.
- **Harbor Reef Saloon** — Rub elbows with sailors, hikers, and locals over a cold beer and casual bites. It's the social hub of Two Harbors.
- **The General Store & Snack Bar** — Perfect for grabbing provisions, a quick sandwich, or ice cream to enjoy by the water.

**What to Do**

- Snorkel or scuba dive the protected coves and kelp forests
- Kayak or paddleboard between the twin harbors
- Hike a stretch of the legendary Trans-Catalina Trail
- Book a guided interior tour for the best chance at bison sightings
- Charter a boat for fishing or coastal exploration
- Simply unwind—claim a spot on the beach and let island time take over

---

*Two Harbors proves that Catalina's greatest treasures lie beyond the crowds. # Two Harbors: Catalina's Wild, Windswept Secret

*Where the crowds thin, the water clears, and the island shows its untamed heart*

---

The ferry cuts across the San Pedro Channel just after dawn, and by the time the Isthmus comes into view—that impossibly narrow neck of land where the Pacific nearly meets itself—you understand why they call this place Two Harbors. On one side, the calm crescent of Isthmus Cove. On the other, the rugged sweep of Catalina Harbor. Between them: barely half a mile of golden hillside, a smattering of buildings, and a pace of life that hasn't changed much in a century.

This is Catalina Island's other town—the one that isn't Avalon. And on a bright September morning, with the fog burning off and the smell of eucalyptus drifting down from the ridgelines, it feels like a place time forgot on purpose.

## Morning: Paddling Into Glass

The best way to meet Two Harbors is from the water, so I start where the locals suggest—slipping a kayak into Isthmus Cove while the surface is still mirror-smooth.

"Morning is everything here," says Marcus Delgado, a longtime paddle guide who has worked these waters for over a decade. "The wind picks up in the afternoon, so if you want that glassy water and the best chance of seeing wildlife, you're launching by eight. This is when the harbor belongs to you."

He's not exaggerating. Within twenty minutes I've drifted past anchored sailboats swaying gently on their moorings and nosed my kayak toward the kelp forests that fringe the shoreline. Peering over the gunwale, the water is startlingly clear—shafts of light spearing down through amber kelp fronds where garibaldi, California's flame-orange state fish, flicker like sparks.

A curious harbor seal surfaces a paddle's length away, regards me with liquid eyes, and vanishes with a soft plosh. Overhead, a brown pelican folds its wings and drops into the cove like a thrown stone.

"People come expecting Avalon and get surprised," Delgado laughs. "Here it's just you, the kelp, and maybe a sea lion following you around because he's bored. It's the Catalina people forget still exists."

## Midday: Into the Hills

By late morning the sun has climbed high enough to warm the trails, and Two Harbors reveals its second personality—rugged, dry, and gloriously empty.

The **Trans-Catalina Trail** threads directly through the Isthmus, and even a short out-and-back delivers sweeping payoffs. I take the climb toward the ridge above Catalina Harbor, switchbacking up through prickly pear and silver-green sage. Within half an hour the whole island geography snaps into focus: two harbors below, the mainland a hazy suggestion to the east, and Catalina's spine rolling away west in folds of chaparral.

Then, movement on the hillside. A bison—yes, a bison—lifts its enormous shaggy head from grazing and stares me down.

"They're the island's most famous accident," explains Dr. Helen Vasquez, a conservation biologist who studies Catalina's ecosystems. "Fourteen bison were brought over for a film shoot in the 1920s and simply left behind. Now they're an icon. But please—give them room. They look like slow, gentle furniture. They are not. A bison can outrun you without trying."

I give the animal the wide, respectful berth Dr. Vasquez recommends and continue along the ridge. She'd told me to watch for the island's subtler residents, too—the Catalina Island fox, a house-cat-sized creature found nowhere else on Earth.

"The fox is the real conservation story," she says. "They crashed to near-extinction and came roaring back—one of the fastest recoveries of any endangered species. If you see one trot across the trail, understand you're looking at a genuine miracle."

I don't spot a fox today, but a red-tailed hawk wheeling on a thermal feels like a fair consolation.

## Afternoon: Local Color at the Isthmus

Back down at sea level, Two Harbors' entire "downtown" can be crossed in a two-minute stroll. There's a general store, a dive shop, a handful of tent cabins scattered up the hillside—and the beating heart of it all, the **Harbor Reef Restaurant**, presided over by a cheerfully weathered building and an even more cheerful clientele of sailors, campers, and sunburned day-trippers.

The signature move here is a drink called **Buffalo Milk**—a creamy, boozy island concoction of vodka, Kahlúa, crème de banana, and whipped cream that tastes nothing like milk and everything like vacation.

"You can't leave without one," insists Sandra Whitfield, who has bartended at the restaurant for years. "First-timers order it as a joke and then order a second one seriously. It's basically the island's official handshake."

The vibe is unhurried and unpretentious—yacht crews trading stories with weekend campers, a dog asleep in a patch of sun, the clink of glasses and the creak of the dock. Nobody's checking a phone. There's barely any signal to check.

"What we've got here is scarcity, and that's the luxury," Whitfield says, nodding toward the cove. "No traffic. No chain stores. When the last ferry leaves, it's just the people staying the night and about a million stars. That's the whole pitch."

## Evening: The Last Light

As the afternoon wind finally kicks up—right on schedule, just as Delgado promised—whitecaps freckle the outer cove and the sailboats tug at their lines. I climb a short rise to watch the sun drop toward Catalina Harbor, the water shifting from turquoise to pewter to burnished gold.

Two Harbors doesn't overwhelm you. It doesn't try. There are no attractions in the theme-park sense—just water clear enough to see your own shadow, hills wild enough to hide bison and foxes, and a rhythm slow enough to remember what unhurried actually feels like.

The last ferry horn sounds across the Isthmus. Most of the day-trippers file aboard. And the ones who stay watch the boat shrink toward the mainland, then turn back toward the hills, the stars already beginning to prick through the dusk.

---

## ✦ TRAVELER'S SIDEBAR: Making the Most of Two Harbors ✦

**GETTING THERE**
- Catalina Express ferries run from San Pedro; the crossing takes roughly an hour. Boats to Two Harbors are less frequent than to Avalon—**check the schedule carefully and book ahead**, especially in summer.
- Seasonal cross-island shuttles connect Avalon and Two Harbors for those wanting both.

**BEST TIME TO VISIT**
- **Spring and fall** offer warm water, thinner crowds, and calmer mornings.
- Summer is liveliest but busiest; winter is quiet and moody, with the fewest services running.

**ON THE WATER**
- **Kayak and snorkel early**—winds reliably build in the afternoon.
- Rentals and guided trips are available at the harborside dive and kayak shop; reserve in advance on weekends.
- Water is clearest around the kelp beds; bring a wetsuit outside of peak summer.

**HIKING NOTES**
- The **Trans-Catalina Trail** passes right through the Isthmus—do a short section even if you're only there for the day.
- A **free hiking permit** is required (available online through the Catalina Island Conservancy).
- Carry more water than you think you need. Shade is scarce and the trails are exposed.

**WILDLIFE ETIQUETTE**
- **Never approach bison.** Stay at least 150 feet away—they're faster and stronger than they look.
- The endangered Catalina Island fox is protected; observe, don't feed.
- Store all food securely; foxes and ravens are enterprising thieves.

**WHERE TO REFUEL**
- **Harbor Reef Restaurant** is the main dining spot—don't skip the legendary **Buffalo Milk** cocktail.
- The **general store** stocks snacks, sunscreen, and camping basics, but selection is limited. Bring essentials from the mainland.

**STAYING OVERNIGHT**
- Options are limited and rustic: waterfront tent cabins, a small lodge, and popular **campgrounds** (reserve well ahead).
- **Cell service is minimal to nonexistent.** Download maps and tickets before you arrive—and consider that a feature, not a bug.

**PRO TIP**
- Day-trippers must watch ferry times closely; missing the last boat means an unplanned (if magical) overnight. If you *can* stay the night, do—the stargazing alone is worth it.

---

*Two Harbors rewards the traveler willing to slow down. Come for the kayaking, stay for the silence, and leave with sand in your shoes and a Buffalo Milk grin.*

# Where the Wild Things Roam: Catalina's Untamed West End

There's a moment, just after sunrise on the west end of Catalina Island, when the world feels newly made. I'm standing barefoot on a crescent of pale sand at Parson's Landing, coffee steaming in a tin cup, watching the Pacific unspool in sheets of hammered silver. No boat horns. No boardwalk clatter. Just the rhythmic hush of waves and the distant bark of something wild carried on the salt breeze. This is the Catalina most visitors never see—the quiet edge of the island, where the famous casino and crowded Avalon harbor feel a hundred miles away instead of a scenic twenty.

## Beneath the Surface

Wade into these waters and the real magic reveals itself. Just offshore, giant kelp forests rise from the seafloor like submerged cathedrals, their amber fronds swaying in the current, reaching sixty feet toward the sunlight. Snorkeling here feels like flying over an alien landscape—shafts of light filtering through the canopy, garibaldi flashing their impossible orange against the green, and the occasional bright-eyed harbor seal materializing from the shadows to study you before darting away.

The kelp is the island's lifeblood, a nursery and pantry for everything from sheephead to sea urchins. On a calm day, drop into the shallows near **Emerald Bay** and you'll understand why divers travel across the world to explore these protected waters. The visibility can stretch beyond a hundred feet, clear as blown glass.

## The Sea Lions of Ship Rock

By late morning, I've traded fins for a kayak, paddling the rugged coastline toward **Ship Rock**, a jagged sea stack that erupts from the channel like a broken tooth. Long before I reach it, I hear them—a chorus of grunts, barks, and belching complaints echoing across the water. California sea lions haul out here by the dozens, jostling for the best sunning spots, their sleek bodies glistening as they flop and squabble.

Keep a respectful distance and they'll reward you with a show: young pups porpoising through the swells, curious juveniles surfacing beside your kayak to blow whiskery breaths in your direction. There's a comedy to them, all bluster and belly, but watch one torpedo through the kelp and you remember these are creatures perfectly built for this coastline.

## Ghosts of the Golden Age

The most unexpected residents of Catalina's west end aren't found in the water at all. They're the buffalo—American bison, to be precise—that roam the island's rolling interior grasslands. A herd of fourteen was brought over in 1924 for a Hollywood Western film shoot and simply... stayed. Today, their descendants, numbering around 150, graze the golden hills like a fever dream of the American plains transplanted to a Pacific island.

Driving the rugged interior roads toward **Little Harbor**, I round a bend and there they are—a half-dozen bison, massive and unbothered, cropping the dry grass against a backdrop of turquoise sea. It's a surreal collision of worlds, the Old West meeting the deep blue, and it's utterly, wonderfully Catalina. Give them plenty of room; a bull can weigh a ton and move faster than you'd think.

As afternoon softens into evening, I make my way back to camp. A hawk wheels overhead. The kelp beds glow copper in the low light. Somewhere out at Ship Rock, the sea lions are still arguing. Out here on the wild west end, you don't visit the island so much as surrender to it—and that, I've decided, is exactly the point.

---

## Best of the West End: A Resource Guide

**Getting There**
- **Catalina Express** ferries run from Long Beach, San Pedro, and Dana Point to Avalon and Two Harbors. For the west end, book passage to **Two Harbors**—the quieter gateway.
- From Two Harbors, reach remote spots via the **Cyclone shore boat**, kayak, or the island's interior roads (permit required for hiking/biking).

**Where to Stay**
- **Two Harbors Campground** – Beachfront tent sites steps from the water.
- **Parson's Landing** – Primitive, blissfully isolated camping with included firewood and water. Reserve well ahead.
- **Banning House Lodge** – A charming 12-room historic inn for those who prefer a roof and a hot shower.

**What to Do**
- **Snorkeling & Diving** – Emerald Bay and Isthmus Cove offer world-class kelp forest exploration. Gear rentals available in Two Harbors.
- **Kayaking** – Paddle to Ship Rock for sea lion viewing (maintain a safe distance).
- **Hiking the Trans-Catalina Trail** – The west-end sections deliver bison sightings and staggering ocean views. Free permits via the Catalina Island Conservancy.
- **Wildlife Tours** – Book a Conservancy-led interior excursion for the best (and safest) buffalo encounters.

**Where to Eat & Drink**
- **Harbor Reef Restaurant** – Two Harbors' beloved spot for fresh seafood and its legendary "Buffalo Milk" cocktail.
- **West End Snack Bar** – Casual bites, cold drinks, and toes-in-the-sand ambiance.

**Know Before You Go**
- Cell service is spotty to nonexistent—embrace the disconnect.
- Pack layers; ocean breezes turn evenings cool.
- All island wildlife is protected. Observe, photograph, and never feed.
- Water is precious out here. Conserve accordingly.

*Best season: Late spring through early fall for calm seas and clear water. Book camping and lodging months in advance.*

# Escape to Two Harbors: Catalina's Quiet Corner

*A 2008 Travel Feature*

While most visitors to Catalina Island crowd the bustling streets of Avalon, those seeking a more tranquil experience should point their compass toward Two Harbors, the rustic village nestled at the island's narrow isthmus. Here, where the Pacific nearly severs the island in two, you'll find a Catalina largely unchanged by time—a place where the pace slows and nature takes center stage.

## The Bison of Catalina

Perhaps no story captures the island's peculiar charm better than that of its resident bison. Visitors are often startled to encounter these massive American icons roaming the interior hills—hardly the wildlife one expects on a California island.

The bison arrived in 1924, brought over as extras for a Hollywood film production. As island lore has it, the crew departed without their shaggy stars, and the animals were left to fend for themselves. Adapt they did. What began as a small herd flourished in Catalina's rugged interior, becoming one of the island's most beloved and photographed attractions. Today's descendants continue to graze the hillsides, a living legacy of the silver screen.

## Conquering the Boushay Trail to Silver Peak

For the adventurous hiker, the challenging trek to Silver Peak offers a rewarding test of endurance. The Boushay Trail winds upward through changing terrain, demanding both stamina and sturdy footwear. This is not a casual stroll—the ascent is steep and the path uneven, but those who persevere are rewarded with breathtaking panoramas of the surrounding channel and, on clear days, views that stretch toward the mainland.

Pack plenty of water, wear proper hiking boots, and allow ample time for the round trip. The solitude of the trail is part of its appeal; you may find yourself entirely alone with the wind, the wildflowers, and the occasional soaring hawk.

## Where to Rest Your Head

After a day of exploration, **The Banning House Lodge** provides the perfect retreat. This historic bed-and-breakfast, perched on a hilltop overlooking both harbors, exudes old-Catalina character with its comfortable rooms and warm hospitality. The lodge offers a refined yet unpretentious base from which to enjoy the isthmus.

*For reservations, call The Banning House Lodge at (310) 510-4228.*

## Dining at Harbor Reef Restaurant

When hunger calls, **Harbor Reef Restaurant** is the heart of Two Harbors' dining scene. Known for its fresh seafood and legendary "Buffalo Milk" cocktail, this waterfront eatery serves up hearty fare in a relaxed, tropical atmosphere. Whether you're refueling after the Silver Peak climb or simply savoring the sunset over the water, it's an essential stop.

*Reservations recommended: call Harbor Reef Restaurant at (310) 510-4215.*

## Getting There

Two Harbors is accessible by ferry, offering a scenic crossing that sets the tone for the unhurried days ahead. Leave the crowds behind and discover the Catalina that time forgot.

---

*Note: Please verify current phone numbers and business details before your trip, as services and contact information may change.*
